newsitem.title: FRANCE: French finance minister stands by economic rigour.
newsitem.headline: French finance minister stands by economic rigour.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on Monday praised Prime Minister Alain Juppe for courageously carrying out a "dirty job" of shaking up the economy and said his policy of economic rigour remains valid.

Arthuis called on Juppe's supporters to keep the faith ahead of next Sunday's final ballot in France's parliamentary election, even though Juppe said on Monday he would stand down whatever the outcome, following a first-round swing to the left.

"We have conducted our campaign on an (economic) programme which remains valid," Arthuis told reporters, asked at an OECD meeting whether the ruling centre-right would try a new tack after the first round turn against the centre-right.

France's opposition Socialist party took a surprise lead in Sunday's first round and is now seen as having a chance of taking power as the centre-right tries to contend with an electorate disappointed by its promises to tackle record 12.8 percent unemployment and its economic policy of austerity.

"I have no regrets about the economic policy we have conducted, but doubtless we will have to go faster, stronger and further," Arthuis, mobbed by reporters as he wound up a news conference on the first day of an OECD ministerial meeting.
"We must clarify our policies, our vision of the world and what we are doing for employment," he said.
Arthuis paid homage to Juppe as a courageous leader who had stuck by what was needed for France and prepared it for Europe's single currency project by getting the economy into shape.

"He has worked for two years to get France back on the rails -- a dirty job, I would say," he said. Juppe's announcement that he would stand down whoever won the next round was a "personal decision...an act of courage".
He declined to say who should replace Juppe if the centre-right managed to keep power, saying the choice was up to President Jacques Chirac.

He also sidestepped questions about his own future in any centre-right administration, saying he would join in the campaign for the next round and put himself at the service of policies he continued to defend.

Arthuis said earlier he was confident voters would turn out for the ruling centre-right coalition in next Sunday's run-off and dismissed any talk of serious pressure on the franc between electoral rounds.

"I don't expect anything like that and I declare my conviction that there will be a mobilisation for the second round," he said. "A message has been sent to the majority (parties) and I think it has been received loud and clear."
